title: Zooming All the Way Out: Thinking in Phases
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing in the middle of COVID school closures, Dave Stuart Jr. offers a tentative framework for teachers and leaders. Phase 1 is the emergency question of delivering accessible remote education, which he argues should be satisficed rather than perfected because it is temporary and expertise develops slowly. Phase 2, the return to buildings, is a severe version of the oldest question: how to close opportunity and achievement gaps. For teachers he advises humane schedules, reaching disengaged students, and protecting an hour a week for professional learning in the science of learning. For leaders he urges mastering the mechanics of reaching families, planning to solve summer, and starting to remove curriculum creation from teachers' jobs. He repeatedly flags his own low confidence and asks readers to test his advice.
points: Satisficing the emergency phase frees time and attention to prepare for the harder, longer-lasting problem of unequal outcomes.
Focusing on what one can control, illustrated with Frankl, guards against the time-wasting and demoralizing habit of predicting when closures will end.
Teachers should protect weekly time for learning about how learning works so Phase 2 does not find them without a shared knowledge base.
Leaders should centralize creation of quality, evidence-informed curricula so teachers can concentrate on instruction, without imposing scripted lessons.
quotes: Speculating on when and how it will end produces terrible returns on the time invested, so it’s best to avoid doing that.
Since Phase 1 is not permanent, it does not make sense for individual teachers or schools to give 100% of their energies to perfecting it.
Phase 2 won’t be about answering a new question, it will be about answering a severe form of our oldest question.
Develop a schedule that offers the lowest likelihood that you’ll go insane during this time.
I think the goal of Phase 1 for teachers should be to provide an at-least-okay set of weekly learning experiences to as many students as possible.
We need fewer responsibilities in curriculum creation so that we might do better on our responsibilities around instruction.
In closing, remember how I started: I’m not The Guy Who Has All the Answers right now. Take these thoughts for what they’re worth.
